title: Westbrook City Council — Special Meeting
note: This summary highlights the meeting's key discussions and decisions, with direct quotes and timestamps for verification — it is not a substitute for watching the full meeting. Summarization necessarily condenses and selects; for complete context, nuance, and anything not covered here, watch the full video at the link above. (Produced by: WestbrookCurrents.com)
attendance: Present: President Jennifer Munro, Vice President Michael Shaughnessy, Brian McCambridge, Victor Chau, Anna Turcotte, Amy Faulkingham (recorded absent for votes from 1:33:44 on), Gary Rairdon. Mayor David Morse also attended.

blocks.x: Remarks on Minneapolis, Immigrant Neighbors & Holiday Lights

Mayor David Morse opened by acknowledging the recent killing in Minneapolis. He said he was “still processing it” like many residents. He repeated a message of support for Westbrook's immigrant neighbors: “I don't feel safer because of ICE... I feel safe when my community and my neighbors are coming together.”

Holiday lights: the city has spent an estimated $180,000 since 2017 upgrading the holiday light display. Downtown tax increment financing, which sets aside tax from new development for that district's projects, separately paid about $88,000 for the animated tree (2021). In both 2023 and 2024, the operating budget got a boost of about $25,000 to enhance the display. The city now spends about $5,000 annually on replacement bulbs and strands, driven largely by vandalism (roughly 20 strands cut per year).

Informational presentation on three city-owned parcels: Cornelia Warren Field, a field referred to as Fraser Field, and the Westbrook High School field. They were permitted to receive biosolids (treated sewage sludge) in the mid-1980s and may contain per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS). The field names are as spoken in the recording. The PFAS slides were not in the packet.

Rip Patton (Credere Associates, the City's Brownfields Qualified Environmental Professional) and Deputy Director of Economic & Community Development Monique Cornett briefed the Council. Project Manager Robyn Saunders gave an initial presentation in January 2025. Since then, the city confirmed a permit existed for biosolid spreading at these sites. But it found no documentation confirming it occurred, or how extensively. The Maine Department of Environmental Protection (DEP) ranks known PFAS sludge sites Tier 1–4 by documented volume. These three are unranked/Tier 4 (not a current DEP priority) because no sludge-spreading has been confirmed.

The City's Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) Brownfields assessment grant turned out to be ineligible for this work. The reason is that the city already owned the parcels when the alleged spreading occurred. Greater Portland Council of Governments Brownfields funds look viable instead, pending an eligibility review (about 2 months). If approved, proposed work includes incremental sampling methodology across each site's surface, plus discrete soil borings at depth (geoprobe, backfilled the same day), at roughly $800 per boring. The plan calls for drilling and sampling in March–April, lab analysis (3 weeks), and a report (2 weeks). Results are expected around May 2026.

“We talk about this in such scientific terms, but we never really discussed what it actually can cause and can mean to a human or an animal... it's kind of shocking to me that there's kind of a blasé attitude toward PFAS from the city administration. It's very harmful.”

Patton acknowledged PFAS is a suspected carcinogen (a cancer-causing substance), though not EPA-confirmed, linked to liver-function and other health effects. But he distinguished the soil testing proposed here from direct ingestion risk, such as PFAS in drinking water. Councilor Faulkingham asked whether a high concentration finding would raise these sites' DEP tier. Patton said he'd assume so but wasn't certain.
Assistant City Administrator Posting, Presumpscot 2040 & Community Food Pantry

Councilor Gary Rairdon objected to the City posting an Assistant City Administrator position. He noted the duties were previously split into the current City Administrator's role as a succession plan. He asked the administration to withdraw the posting. He said he'd revisit the position during the next budget review.

Vice President Michael Shaughnessy announced “Presumpscot 2040,” a public-input process on the Presumpscot River (water quality, recreation, habitat, culture). It is run by the Casco Bay Estuary Partnership and facilitated by Craig Freshley. It has two public sessions on Feb. 2, 2026 at the Westbrook Community Center (2:30–5:00 PM and 6:30–9:00 PM).
President Jennifer Munro echoed the Mayor's remarks on the national mood. She highlighted a new free food pantry, “Cater to Community,” at Mr. Bagel on Main Street.
Extensive public comment, almost entirely about Order 2026-02 (rifle suppressors, see next section). There was also brief comment on the separate Dory Schollberger/12 Water Street matter.

Spoke on Legislative Document (LD) 1829 and the Dory Schollberger/12 Water Street matter. Then he cautioned the Mayor and Council against any implication of opposing federal law enforcement in their remarks on immigration: “We don't want Minneapolis to happen here... we who believe in legal immigration but oppose illegal immigration, we don't want that [either].” Not discussed further by the Council on the record.

The Clerk read four letters into the record. They were from Amanda Hollander (Ward 4), John Scribner (on the Water Street matter, unrelated to the suppressor order), Mary Tardiff (Ward 2), and Carrie Tyson (237 Bridge St., a U.S. Air Force veteran). See the Order 2026-02 section below for the substance.
Orders of the Day — Second & Final Reading
Orders 2026-03, 2026-04 — CCTV Software Subscription & Replacement Tractor (Consent)

These orders were up for second and final reading, the final, binding vote. Moved together by Councilor Rairdon. President Munro pulled Order 2026-02 (rifle suppressors) out for separate debate, covered next. Order 2026-03 approves buying closed-circuit-television (CCTV) inspection software. Order 2026-04 approves replacing a utility tractor. No discussion on either.
Both approved together by unanimous roll call, 7–0. Moved by Gary Rairdon, seconded by Anna Turcotte.
Order 2026-02 — Rifle Suppressors for the Police Department

Second and final reading. The first reading, the first of two required votes, passed 6–0 on Jan. 5, 2026. The order buys 50 rifle suppressors for a combined price of $24,405.50. It is paid entirely from the Police Department's federal forfeiture funds (no local tax dollars). Note: the packet's narrative memo names the vendor as Energetic Armament/Energetic Arms of Mattapoisett, MA. But the order's own legal text and itemized quote list name the low bidder as Summit Sound Technologies, LLC, also of Mattapoisett, MA. The quote list matches the final $24,405.50 total exactly. This inconsistency exists in the City's own packet and is noted here, not resolved.

“Not a single U.S. military branch utilizes suppressors for weapon system validation... Suppressors are provided only to Tier One special operations units in the military in order to prevent muzzle flash in combat zones... This feels as if we are further trending toward the continued militarization of our police force under the guise of enhancing PPE.”

“I don't want our cops to look like ICE and I don't want them to start using the tactics of ICE... I have not had a clear sidewalk a single day this year... I have to imagine that it wouldn't take too many silencers['-worth of funds] to pay for just clearing the snow on the sidewalks.”

“Studies do show that when police forces have more militarized equipment, that they're more likely to have violent encounters with the public, irrespective of local crime rates... I think all gun accessories... I see them as toys for men.”

Four letters were also read into the record. Three (Amanda Hollander, Mary Tardiff, and U.S. Air Force veteran Carrie Tyson) opposed or conditioned support on the order. They questioned the $24,405.50 price, the need for 50 units, and whether cheaper hearing-protection alternatives existed. A fourth, from John Scribner, was on the unrelated Water Street matter.

“Let me assure you, as a former refugee and someone who's lived outside of this country, that... America is [not] the only country where police use[s] force. That is incorrect... What happened in Minneapolis... is completely unrelated to the police department that we have in this city... I am also very hesitant to believe that this is about cost. We had paid more for the leather chairs at the library than these suppressors... Let's not pretend that this is about cost or it is about Minneapolis. This is a different kind of agenda. I don't appreciate it. You guys should come out and say what actually is on your minds.”

“Guns are there, especially within the police department, [to] protect us from criminals, protect our children from school shooters... I don't know what kind of world you live in, but I appreciate all those men with guns that protect us.”

The department has 49 officers, each issued a personally zeroed (sighted-in) rifle, plus one spare, hence 50 units. Lally drew a firm distinction between suppressors and movie-style “silencers,” which don't exist for rifles. Suppressors reduce noise but don't eliminate it, by roughly 25–40 decibels off a ~160-decibel unsuppressed rifle. He cited his own military-service hearing loss as part of his motivation. He framed the purchase as personal protective equipment rather than militarization, noting the department deliberately avoids armored vehicles and similar gear. He disclosed that Westbrook officers on the Cumberland County Emergency Services Unit, a regional tactical team, already carry Westbrook-owned, suppressor-equipped rifles on the street weekly. Rank-and-file officers currently train with rifles only twice a year (June and October/November) due to budget limits. He noted the Eleanor Ave. range has drawn noise complaints from abutters, meaning neighboring property owners. Councilor Faulkingham asked whether this is standard elsewhere. Lally and Rairdon said Lewiston and Gorham police departments either have or are acquiring suppressors, as does the Cumberland County Sheriff's Department.
“I don't really see a benefit to having it be less quiet in a neighborhood if there is actual gunfire. If there's gonna be gunfire in a neighborhood, I wanna know — to stay away, to stay indoors.”

President Munro pressed further on federal-forfeiture-fund spending rules. Lally confirmed the funds can cover firearms and accessories but not salaries or replacing budgeted positions. He also said the department is audited annually with a full inventory requirement. Vice President Shaughnessy said he had been “quite on the fence” given “the times that we're in” but wanted to support it after Lally's explanation. Councilor Chau said he was “supporting this based on the safety impact on the officers, not on anything else.” Councilor McCambridge asked whether this would increase training frequency. Lally said he would like somewhat more, but range access and cost are limiting.

Order 2026-02 passed [1:23:21] 6–1, with President Jennifer Munro the lone dissenting vote. Moved by Gary Rairdon, seconded by Anna Turcotte. For: Michael Shaughnessy, Brian McCambridge, Victor Chau, Turcotte, Amy Faulkingham, Rairdon. Against: Munro.
Found on page 28 of the packet.

Moved by Councilor Rairdon under 21-A Maine Revised Statutes Annotated §503, as recommended by the City Clerk and Registrar of Voters. A Resolve is a formal statement or decision by the Council (Westbrook's term).
Approved by unanimous roll call, 7–0. Moved by Gary Rairdon, seconded by Victor Chau.
Resolve 2026-04 — Zoning Board of Appeals — Cliff McCarthy
Found on page 33 of the packet.

Confirms Mayor Morse's appointment of Cliff McCarthy as an alternate member of the Zoning Board of Appeals. He is an experienced appellate attorney and a recent Ward 4 transplant. The term runs for the remainder of a three-year term expiring Dec. 31, 2026.
Approved by unanimous roll call, 7–0. Moved by Gary Rairdon, seconded by Victor Chau.
Found on page 36 of the packet.

Read by title only at Councilor Chau's request, since the Council had discussed it at length at a prior meeting. Councilor Rairdon asked to confirm what a “yes” vote meant. He was told it sends a message to Westbrook's legislative delegation supporting amendments toward the resolve's stated goals.
Approved by unanimous roll call, 7–0. Moved by Victor Chau, seconded by Amy Faulkingham.
Order 2026-05 — Criminal Forfeiture Asset — Ruger AR-15 Rifle
Found on page 46 of the packet.

Approves transfer of a Ruger AR-15 rifle (serial no. 85387398) for continued Police Department use rather than destruction. The rifle was forfeited to the department through a Cumberland County Unified Criminal Court drug-trafficking/overdose-death case (Docket No. CR-22-744). Chief Lally explained the department typically destroys non-usable forfeited firearms (roughly 100–150 last year). It adopts serviceable, matching-caliber weapons like this one to avoid a roughly $1,500 replacement purchase. He said the department is otherwise well-stocked on rifles for the next 5–10 years.
Approved 6–0 (Councilor Faulkingham absent for this and the remaining votes). Moved by Gary Rairdon, seconded by Victor Chau.
Order 2026-06 — Credere Associates Task Order No. 7 — Riverwalk North Survey (First Reading)
Found on page 51 of the packet.

Authorizes a $36,100 update to the City's 2015 Riverwalk North topographic survey. The work goes through subcontractor Owen Haskell, Inc. of Falmouth, ME. It is needed because a wetland/invasive-species assessment, floodplain changes, and regulatory updates have occurred since 2015.
Passed first reading, unanimous roll call, 6–0. Moved by Victor Chau, seconded by Gary Rairdon.
Order 2026-07 — Sigma Tactical Wellness Health & Wellness Screenings (First Reading)
Found on page 55 of the packet.

Authorizes an agreement, up to $41,000, with Sigma Tactical Wellness (Austin, TX) for voluntary health and wellness screenings for police, fire, and dispatch personnel. The screenings are a carotid intima-media thickness ultrasound, a cardiac stress test, and a telehealth consult with a healthcare provider. It is primarily funded through a Maine Department of Public Safety grant (Order 2025-114). The balance is split between the Fire Department's medical-exam line and the Police Department's federal forfeiture line. Fire Chief Stephen Sloan explained the screening menu in response to Councilor Chau's question.
Passed first reading, unanimous roll call, 6–0. Moved by Victor Chau, seconded by Brian McCambridge.
No further public comment; no referrals or committee reports.
Motion to adjourn approved by unanimous roll call, 6–0. Moved by Victor Chau, seconded by Gary Rairdon.

howMade: This summary was produced from the meeting video (linked above, hosted on the City's Vimeo showcase). The audio was transcribed with AI-assisted speech-to-text and speaker identification. This process cross-checked names and figures against the official packet and the city council roster, attributed speakers from context (introductions, roll-call order, direct address by the presiding officer) rather than the raw diarization labels alone, and drafted this summary and the quoted excerpts. Quotes are lightly cleaned of filler words/false starts but not reworded. Reviewed by Gerald Doyon. A separate AI accuracy check then compared this summary against the transcript and agenda packet. Errors it found were corrected, and Gerald Doyon verified against the meeting video the points only the video could settle.
